pages.title: See Your Kitchen Three Ways Before You Touch a Wall
pages.intro: Upload one room, describe the direction, and see it before you spend a dollar on it.
pages.problemTitle: Not Sure a New Look Is Worth the Cost of Finding Out?
pages.problem: Committing to a full redo on a hunch is how "small refresh" turns into "took out a loan." Most of that risk disappears once you can actually see the direction first.
pains: A color or material you loved in a showroom that looked completely different at home
A contractor quote that assumes a finish you never actually confirmed you wanted
Not knowing if "just paint and hardware" will actually read as different enough
Committing to tile before seeing it next to the counter you're keeping
A Pinterest board full of kitchens that cost five times your actual budget
benefits: One Room, Real Constraints
Briller works from your actual kitchen, not a generic layout
Plain-Language Brief
describe what's bothering you, no design vocabulary required
Try Before You Buy
compare two or three directions before committing to any of them
steps: one photo of the kitchen as it is today
Briller generates a direction styled to your actual room
not right? Adjust the brief and try again
HD image, ready to compare against a contractor's quote
advice: White oak veneer cabinet fronts, honed quartz counter (~2cm)
3000K LED strip under the upper cabinets
Reface only — this design assumes your existing cabinet boxes stay, which is what keeps it in spot-renovation budget territory.
directions: existing boxes kept, fronts and hardware swapped
same layout, new tile pattern and grout color
no material changes, just color and hardware direction
briefs: Keep the layout, just make it feel warmer and less dated
Show me this kitchen with white oak cabinets instead of the dark wood
I want more counter space without moving anything structural
pages.note: This level of detail is part of Pro Design — Explorer gives you Smart Sparks, Briller's faster, plainer-language pointers, not a full materials breakdown. Renders assume your existing cabinet boxes and layout stay put; anything involving moving plumbing or walls needs Pro Design's fuller notes at minimum, plus a contractor.
faqs: Does this work if my kitchen is already fully furnished?
Yes — Briller works from the room as it is, furniture and all.
How many directions can I try?
Try directions within your available credits. The app shows the cost of an action before you run it.
Do I need to know design terms to write a brief?
No — plain language like "warmer" or "less cluttered" works.
Is this the same detail level as Pro Design?

Start with Free for basic exploration. Explorer includes basic Smart Sparks; Pro Design and Studio / Architect include full Briller Insights. Compare the current plans for credits, exports and team features.

pages.title: Plan Every Room Without Losing Track of Any of Them
pages.intro: One project per room, each with its own history — so three renovations don't turn into one blur.
pages.problemTitle: Renovating Room by Room and Losing Track of What You Decided?
pages.problem: A whole-home renovation isn't one decision, it's forty small ones, spread across months and usually across more than one contractor. Losing track of what you already decided is how budgets creep.
pains: Forgetting which flooring you picked for the hallway versus the bedroom
Two contractors quoting against two different versions of "the plan"
A material decided on in March that nobody can find by June
Losing the thread on what's already budgeted vs. still undecided
A whole-home vision that looks cohesive in your head, incoherent on paper
benefits: One Project Per Room
kitchen, primary bath, basement, each tracked separately
Full History, Not Just the Latest Version
every Refine saved
Unlimited Projects
nothing capped while you're mid-renovation
HD, Contractor-Ready Downloads
no watermark
steps: start a separate project per room
describe the direction for that specific space
Briller generates a direction for each project
advice: 5" wide-plank white oak flooring, engineered, throughout the main living area
2700K dimmable recessed lighting; spacing depends on fixture output and the room
Wide-plank engineered flooring floats over most subfloors — but if underfloor heating is part of the plan, get that spec'd before you buy the flooring, not after.
directions: cabinet and counter direction, tracked independently
flooring direction, shown on its own timeline
briefs: Match the flooring direction from the living room into the hallway
Same cabinet tone as the kitchen, scaled down for the laundry room
Show me this room with the wall opened up, just as a concept
pages.note: Unlimited projects means unlimited rooms, not unlimited scope creep. Structural changes can alter the whole-home budget. Explore the idea, then have an engineer assess the structure and a contractor price the actual scope.
faqs: Can I track a kitchen and two bathrooms at once?
Yes — each is its own project with its own history.
Does Refine history help me stay consistent across rooms?
Yes — you can reference an earlier project's direction in a new brief.
Is there a limit on projects with Pro Design?
No — unlimited projects on this tier.
Can I hand these renders to more than one contractor?
Yes — HD, watermark-free downloads are built for that.
pages.label: Whole-home renovation

pages.title: Make It Feel Like Yours Without Losing the Deposit
pages.intro: Upload the room, describe the direction, explore reversible changes to discuss with your landlord.
pages.problemTitle: Want the Place to Feel Like Yours Without Losing the Deposit?
pages.problem: Most design inspiration assumes you can paint, drill, and renovate freely — a renter's actual constraint is usually the opposite, and most tools don't design around that at all.
pains: A style you love that assumes you can paint or drill wherever you want
Not knowing what's actually reversible versus what risks the security deposit
Command hooks and removable wallpaper that look flimsy in every example photo you find
A landlord who's unclear about what's actually allowed
Wanting the space to feel finished without any permanent investment in someone else's property
benefits: Reversible-Only Direction
every suggestion is designed to come down cleanly
Landlord-Safe Materials Named
command hooks, removable wallpaper, no drilling, stated explicitly
Real Room, Real Constraints
works from your actual rental, not an idealized version
Budget-Aware Styling
a full refresh on a renter's typical budget
steps: the rental space as it stands today
Brief the Direction, Noting It's a Rental
advice: Removable peel-and-stick wallpaper, command-hook gallery wall, freestanding shelving
Plug-in sconces instead of hardwired fixtures, 2700K
Every item here is reversible or landlord-safe — no drilling, no permanent alteration, and no assumption that hardwired lighting can be changed.
directions: reversible pattern applied to an otherwise bare wall
full styling direction using only non-permanent changes
briefs: Style this room using only removable, renter-friendly changes
Add a gallery wall using command hooks only, no drilling
Show this wall with removable wallpaper instead of paint
pages.note: "Reversible" and "landlord-approved" aren't always the same thing — confirm with your actual lease or landlord before applying anything, even removable products.
faqs: Does this guarantee my landlord will approve the changes?
No — confirm with your actual lease or landlord; "reversible" isn't automatically "approved."
Are the suggested products actually removable?
Materials notes name renter-safe options like removable wallpaper and command hooks — always check the specific product's own instructions.
Can I use this for a shared room, not just a full apartment?
Yes — brief the specific room or area.
Is this available on the free plan?

pages.title: Make the Corner You Work From Actually Work
pages.intro: One small room or corner, one small budget, a real difference in how it functions.
pages.problemTitle: Working From a Corner That Doesn't Actually Work?
pages.problem: A home office that's really just a desk wedged into a spare corner tends to stay that way indefinitely, because a full room redesign feels like overkill for a corner.
pains: A desk setup that technically exists and doesn't actually work for a full workday
Glare or bad lighting nobody addresses because it's "just a corner"
Storage that's either nonexistent or eating the room's only open space
A workspace that doesn't feel separate from the rest of the room
A furnishing budget too small to justify hiring a designer for one corner
benefits: Small-Space Focus
built for a corner or spare room, not a dedicated office
Task Lighting Called Out
where the light should actually be, not just how the room looks
Shop the Look
the desk, chair, and shelving, priced and linked
Freestanding-First Direction
minimal to no wall work assumed
steps: the space as it is today
plain language, no design terms needed
a workspace direction within that budget
advice: 4000K task lamp at the desk, 2700K ambient elsewhere in the room
A wall-mounted desk needs to land on studs or use rated anchors — worth checking before you buy it, not after it's on the wall.
directions: unused corner turned into a working desk area
a small closet reimagined as a compact workspace
briefs: Turn this corner into a workspace without changing anything else in the room
Small desk setup that doesn't feel like an office when I'm not working
Add proper task lighting to this desk area
pages.note: A floating desk looks cleaner in a render than a desk with drawers. If you actually need file storage, say so in the brief before you fall for the look.
faqs: Does this require a dedicated room?
No — built for a corner or shared-use space.
Can I see furniture pricing before buying?
Yes — Shop the Look includes name, price, and where to buy.
Is task lighting placement included in the notes?
Yes — Lighting & Ambiance notes call out where light should go.

pages.title: Start From the Actual Floor Plan, Not a Guess at One
pages.intro: Upload blueprints alongside the room photo — dimensions and constraints inform the render, not just the finish.
pages.problemTitle: Tired of Renders That Ignore Your Actual Floor Plan?
pages.problem: Most AI visualization tools generate a plausible-looking room with no relationship to your actual dimensions — fine for inspiration, useless for a client conversation about a real project.
pains: A gorgeous render that ignores where a load-bearing wall actually sits
Client excitement about a layout that doesn't fit their real square footage
Generic finishes that don't reflect the spec you're actually proposing
No way to hand a client something more substantial than a picture
Concept tools that assume every project starts from an empty room
benefits: Blueprint-Aware Generation
dimensions and constraints shape the render
Briller Insights
Explore materials, lighting and implementation questions alongside the concept.
PDF exports
Export specification notes on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
Faster generation queue
Available on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
steps: the actual plan, not a stand-in
describe materials, finish level, or layout intent
adjust and regenerate as the concept develops
advice: 4" structural steel column, clad in blackened steel panel
Linear cove lighting, 3500K, running the perimeter of the exposed ceiling
The column cladding is decorative and non-load-bearing — the column itself is structural, and this render assumes it stays exactly where the blueprint shows it.
directions: existing wall removed as a visualization, structural column called out explicitly
same layout, two finish packages compared
briefs: Show this with the wall opened per the blueprint, column exposed and clad
Same footprint, propose a finish package for a mid-range budget
Match the ceiling height and window placement exactly to the plan
pages.note: A render that ignores your blueprint's dimensions can look great and still be unbuildable in the actual footprint — that gap is the reason this page exists, not the finish. A blueprint can add dimensional context to a concept; it's a concept aid for client conversations, not a stamped structural determination.
faqs: What blueprint formats work?
Standard floor plan uploads alongside the room photo — check current supported formats in-app.

No — it's fast concept alignment before that stage, not a replacement for it.

pages.title: Get the Client to Yes Before You Write the Quote
pages.intro: Show them a direction, hand them a materials list they can actually price against.
pages.problemTitle: Client Loves the Look, Then Balks at the Quote?
pages.problem: The gap between what a client imagines and what a quote actually costs is where deals stall — usually because nobody showed them a real direction before the number.
pains: A client who can't picture the finished room from a verbal description alone
Sticker shock on a quote that reflects a finish they never actually agreed to
Competing bids where the client is comparing apples to oranges
Redoing a proposal because the client's mental image didn't match the plan
No easy way to show two budget tiers side by side
benefits: Client-Ready Renders
a direction to react to before the estimate
Budget-tier comparison
Show a mid-range and premium finish package before pricing the installation.
PDF exports
Export specification notes on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
Faster generation queue
Available on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
steps: the scope you're planning to quote
Refine With the Client in the Room
materials list attached to the proposal
advice: Task lighting under cabinets, 4000K, plus one 2700K pendant over the island
Full-height slab needs a flat substrate and typically two installers — budget for that labor line, it's often left off a first estimate.
directions: same room, two finish packages, shown side by side
existing room next to the proposed direction
briefs: Show the mid-range and the premium version of this kitchen, side by side
Match the finish package we quoted for the economy bid line
Keep the layout, change only the surfaces we're bidding on
pages.note: Renders inform the client conversation — they don't replace a real quote or an engineering sign-off. Say that plainly to the client before the render does the selling for you. The client fell in love with the full-height slab render; the budget says tile to counter height. Show both, name the price gap, let them choose with eyes open.
faqs: Can I show two budget tiers in one client meeting?
Yes — prepare both directions before the meeting, then use feedback to refine the proposal.
Does the PDF export replace my own bid documentation?
No — it's a materials/spec reference to attach alongside your actual bid.

pages.title: The Two Rooms Where the Wrong Material Costs You the Most
pages.intro: Briller's notes go into cabinetry, plumbing, and ventilation — not just the paint color.
pages.problemTitle: One Material Choice Away From Blowing the Whole Budget?
pages.problem: Kitchens and bathrooms carry more of a renovation budget than any other room, and most of that cost lives in decisions that don't show up in a pretty render — substrate, venting, water lines.
pains: A tile choice that looks simple and isn't, labor-wise
Countertop overhang that looks fine in a render and isn't structurally supported
A vent fan relocation nobody priced into the original scope
GFCI placement that becomes an afterthought until inspection
A finish that reads "mid-range" in a photo and prices like "premium"
benefits: Room-Specific Detail
cabinetry construction, edge profiles, tile setting patterns
Plumbing & Electrical Notes
where a vent stack, GFCI, or supply line realistically lands
PDF exports
Export specification notes on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
Faster generation queue
Available on Pro Design and Studio / Architect.
steps: kitchen or bath as it is today
note any layout changes, not just finish preferences
advice: Zellige is hand-formed and irregular — budget 15–20% more tile than a standard rectified job to account for cutting waste, and a setter experienced with it.
directions: layout change shown alongside the finish direction
briefs: Show this bathroom with a curbless shower instead of the tub
Same cabinet boxes, new fronts and hardware only
Full-height tile versus tile-to-counter-height, side by side
pages.note: Handmade tile looks better in every render. It also costs more in labor than the tile itself — the render should say so, not just show it. A render this specific can make a labor-intensive material look like a simple swap; price the install, not just the material, before it goes in a client-facing quote.
faqs: Does this account for plumbing relocation cost?
It notes where fixtures realistically need to land — actual relocation cost still needs your own estimate.
Can I compare a tub-to-shower layout change?
Yes — describe the layout change in the brief and Refine from there.

pages.title: Show a Buyer What the Room Could Be, Not Just What's Empty
pages.intro: Upload a listing photo, stage the room, let the before/after do the work.
pages.problemTitle: Empty Rooms Sitting on the Market?
pages.problem: An empty room reads smaller and colder in photos than it does in person, and most buyers scroll past a listing before they ever picture themselves in it.
pains: A vacant room that photographs smaller than it actually is
Buyers who can't picture furniture placement from an empty photo
Listing photos that get less engagement than staged comparables
A seller who's already moved out, no furniture left to stage with
A tight turnaround between the listing going live and the first showing
benefits: Before/After Slider
the room as it is, and staged, one image
Minutes Per Room
about the time it takes to write the listing description
Beyond Furniture
a stated style direction, not just "add a couch"
Style Range
direction described in plain language to match your buyer pool
steps: the room as it currently stands
style and target buyer, in plain language
staged, photorealistic light and proportions preserved
try a second style before choosing one
advice: Light oak console, linen slipcover sofa, jute rug
Warm 2700K floor lamp, staged for a late-afternoon listing photo
Staging only — nothing here assumes construction, which is worth saying plainly on the listing. Check your local MLS rules on disclosing virtually staged photos.
directions: sofa, rug, and lighting direction added
bed, nightstands, and a warm lighting pass
briefs: Stage this living room for a young family buyer, warm and casual
Modern, minimal staging for this condo, target a first-time buyer
Neutral, broad-appeal staging — nothing too specific to one taste
pages.note: Stage each room in minutes — this isn't a one-pass, whole-listing batch tool today, so budget a few minutes per room rather than one action for the whole property. Virtual staging sells the room's potential, not a fact about what's included in the sale — disclose it as staged, every time.
faqs: Can I stage an entire listing in one action?
Not currently — each room is staged individually.
Do I need to disclose virtual staging?
Check your local MLS and state disclosure rules — this varies by market.
Can I try more than one staging style for the same room?
Yes — Refine to compare styles before choosing one for the listing.

pages.intro: Photograph the rooms that need work, get a direction with real cost logic attached, before you're locked into a purchase.
pages.problemTitle: Not Sure This Flip Actually Pencils Out?
pages.problem: The math on a flip lives or dies on renovation cost, and most of that number gets guessed at during a walkthrough, before anyone's actually priced the work.
pains: A "cosmetic" fix that's actually a subfloor problem in disguise
Two competing offers where the renovation budget is the real unknown
A render-worthy idea that doesn't match the property's actual comps
Underestimating labor on a finish that looks simple in a photo

every room that needs work gets its own project
Cost-Aware Direction
materials and installation notes, not just a nicer photo
Fast Turnaround
a direction in minutes, while you're still deciding on the offer
Budget-Tier Framing
see the realistic version, not just the aspirational one
steps: as many as the walkthrough turns up
a cost-aware direction, not just a prettier photo
compare a light refresh against a fuller renovation

no layout change, surface refresh only

What would this bathroom look like with just paint and fixtures changed
Compare a light refresh against a full gut, same room

Can I compare a light refresh against a full renovation?

Minutes per room, assuming photos are ready.
